newsitem.title: USA: GM invests $40 million in Camaro revamp.
newsitem.headline: GM invests $40 million in Camaro revamp.

text.p: General Motors Corp pegged the investment cost for its revamped 1998 Chevrolet Camaro and Pontiac Firebird sport coupes at about $40 million on Friday, but the auto giant spent far more on the cars' brakes.

The new cars, unveiled Friday at the Chicago Auto Show, feature the Robert Bosch GmBH anti-lock braking system that caused a 17-day strike at two GM brake plants in Dayton, Ohio last year, costing GM about $900 million in lost production.

GM executives said they chose the Bosch system over brakes from its own Delphi Chassis Division -- which supplies brakes for current Camaro and Firebird models -- because they cost less and offered superior technology.
GM waged the strike, which shut down nearly all of its 29 North American assembly plants, in order to preserve its ability to buy parts from outside suppliers.

Ken Ratkovich, Camaro/Firebird program manager, said the $40 million investment figure does not include development cost for the car's aluminum LS1 V-8 engine, which was developed for the new Chevrolet Corvette sports car.

He said Camaro's improvements, which include the engine, brakes, a new front grille and a less harsh ride, should help boost sales 15 to 20 percent above the 66,866 units sold in 1996. He said the program worked to keep investment cost low, because the sporty coupe market is not expected to grow.
"It's very difficult to justify big expenditures without a reasonable rate of return," he said.
